name: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system

reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / CNS vasculitis literature
clinicalPearls: Inflammatory vasculitis confined to the brain, spinal cord, and leptomeningeal vessels without systemic involvement
Presents insidiously with headache, cognitive decline, and recurrent focal deficits over weeks to months
Systemic inflammatory markers are frequently normal, unlike in most systemic vasculitides
Angiography may show a progressive pattern of segmental stenosis and dilatation, but can be normal in small-vessel disease
Cerebrospinal fluid usually shows a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy remains the diagnostic reference standard and helps exclude mimics
Immunosuppression, typically corticosteroids combined with a cytotoxic agent, is the cornerstone of treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system is an idiopathic inflammatory vasculitis restricted to vessels of the brain, spinal cord, and meninges. Segmental infiltration of small and medium arterial walls by lymphocytes, granulomas, or necrotising inflammation leads to vessel wall thickening, luminal narrowing, and thrombosis, producing progressive multifocal ischaemia and occasionally haemorrhage. Because inflammation is patchy and confined to the CNS, systemic markers are typically unremarkable and diagnosis can be difficult, with progressive rather than reversible arterial narrowing distinguishing it from vasoconstrictive syndromes.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary CNS vasculitis from systemic disease or infection
Infective arteritis such as varicella-zoster or tuberculous vasculopathy
Intravascular lymphoma or other neoplastic mimics
additionalInvestigations: Contrast MRI showing multifocal infarcts, white-matter change, or vessel-wall enhancement
Digital subtraction angiography assessing for segmental stenoses with awareness of limited sensitivity
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for lymphocytic pleocytosis and exclusion of infection and malignancy
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy for definitive histological confirmation
Systemic vasculitis and infection screen to exclude secondary causes
redFlags: Progressive encephalopathy with recurrent strokes despite risk-factor control
New intracranial haemorrhage in a young patient
Rapid cognitive deterioration with multifocal deficits
Diagnostic uncertainty where infection or malignancy has not been excluded before immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: Untreated PACNS is often severely disabling or fatal, but many patients stabilise or improve with immunosuppression; relapses occur and outcome depends on prompt diagnosis and treatment.
pitfalls: Confusing it with reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and giving inappropriate immunosuppression
Relying on a normal angiogram or normal inflammatory markers to exclude the diagnosis
Starting immunosuppression before excluding infection and lymphoma
Under-recognising small-vessel disease that spares large arteries on angiography
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Induce remission with high-dose corticosteroids combined with cyclophosphamide
Maintain remission with a steroid-sparing agent such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil
Consider rituximab for refractory or relapsing disease
Exclude and treat mimics such as infection, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, and malignancy before committing to immunosuppression
Monitor disease activity with serial MRI and clinical review, remaining alert to relapse
Provide prophylaxis against treatment complications including Pneumocystis pneumonia, osteoporosis, and gastric ulceration
Institute secondary stroke prevention and vascular risk-factor management with neurorehabilitation
Manage jointly within a neurology and rheumatology multidisciplinary team
